lessons.title: States of matter, particles and diffusion
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Kinetic particle theory, states of matter, diffusion (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the arrangement and motion of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Name the changes of state and explain them with the particle model.
Explain diffusion and why lighter particles diffuse faster.
Interpret melting and boiling points to decide the state of a substance.
reviewNotes: Boiling point of nitrogen −196 °C (77 K) is a standard value.
In the ammonia/hydrogen chloride experiment the white ring forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end: standard result.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The particle model
blocks.md: All matter is made of tiny **particles** (atoms, molecules or ions) that are always moving. In a **solid** the particles are close together in a regular pattern and only **vibrate** about fixed positions. In a **liquid** they are close but irregular and can **slide past** each other. In a **gas** they are far apart, move **randomly and fast**, and fill their container.

blocks.title: Changes of state
blocks.md: **Melting** (solid → liquid), **freezing** (liquid → solid), **boiling/evaporation** (liquid → gas), **condensation** (gas → liquid), **sublimation** (solid → gas directly, e.g. iodine). Heating gives particles more energy; at the melting or boiling point the energy overcomes the forces between particles, so the **temperature stays constant** during the change.

blocks.title: Diffusion
blocks.md: **Diffusion** is the spreading of particles from a region of high concentration to low concentration, by random movement. It is fast in gases, slow in liquids, almost nil in solids. At the same temperature **lighter particles diffuse faster**. Example: ammonia (NH₃) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) gases meet in a tube and form a white ring of ammonium chloride **closer to the HCl end**, because the lighter NH₃ travels further in the same time.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- The particles themselves do **not** expand when a substance is heated; they move faster or further apart.
- Dissolving is not melting.
- A substance is liquid at a given temperature only if that temperature is **between** its melting and boiling points.

blocks.caption: Particle arrangement in a solid (regular, close), a liquid (close, irregular) and a gas (far apart).
blocks.alt: Three boxes of circles: a regular grid for the solid, close random circles for the liquid and few widely spaced circles for the gas.

blocks.title: Example 1 — deciding the state
blocks.statement: A substance melts at −20 °C and boils at 80 °C. What is its state at 25 °C? At 100 °C?
steps: At 25 °C: this is above the melting point (−20 °C) and below the boiling point (80 °C), so the substance is a **liquid**.
At 100 °C: this is above the boiling point, so it is a **gas**.

blocks.title: Example 2 — which diffuses faster?
blocks.statement: Cotton wool with ammonia solution is placed at one end of a long glass tube and cotton wool with hydrochloric acid at the other end. Where does the white ring form and why?
steps: Ammonia gas (NH₃) is lighter than hydrogen chloride gas (HCl), so its particles diffuse faster and travel further.
The gases meet nearer the HCl end, where white ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) forms: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Explain, using the particle model, why a gas can be compressed but a liquid cannot easily be.
exercises.model: In a gas the particles are far apart with a lot of empty space, so they can be pushed closer together. In a liquid the particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to compress.
exercises.rubric: 1 mark: gas particles far apart / empty space; 1 mark: liquid particles already close together.
exercises.explanation: In a gas the particles are far apart with a lot of empty space, so they can be pushed closer together. In a liquid the particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to compress.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: The table gives data for four substances: P (melts −7 °C, boils 59 °C); Q (melts 801 °C, boils 1413 °C); R (melts −219 °C, boils −183 °C); S (melts 0 °C, boils 100 °C). Room temperature is 25 °C.

parts.prompt: Which substance is a gas at room temperature?
parts.explanation: R boils at −183 °C, far below 25 °C, so it is a gas.

parts.prompt: Which substance is a solid at room temperature?
parts.explanation: Q melts at 801 °C, so it is solid at 25 °C.
25 °C lies between the melting and boiling points of both P and S.

parts.prompt: Explain why the temperature of S stays at 100 °C while it boils.
parts.model: The heat energy supplied is used to separate the particles (overcome the forces between them) rather than to raise their average kinetic energy.
parts.rubric: 1 mark: energy used to separate particles; 1 mark: so the temperature does not rise.
parts.explanation: The heat energy supplied is used to separate the particles (overcome the forces between them) rather than to raise their average kinetic energy.
